reading_translation_sentences: Every high position here in the world is surrounded by dangers: just as worldly dignities grow greater, so the dangers grow fiercer.
Thus, from that, we can recognize and understand the examples.

The tree, then, that grows in the woodland so that it towers up above all the other trees and spreads itself, when a storm and a strong wind suddenly strike, is shaken and tossed more violently than the rest of the forest.
It is likewise also with high cliffs and crags: when they tower far up above the rest of the earth, they suddenly begin to fall and crash very violently to the ground.

Likewise also with the high mountains and hills which stand high above the whole world: nevertheless they suffer the penalty of that pre-eminence, namely that they are frequently chastised and beaten by heavenly fire, and struck by thunderbolts.
So the high powers here in the world collapse and fall and come to destruction; the riches of this world turn to sorrow, and these earthly wonders come to nothing.
reading_notes: The opening ār is honour/rank/position, not copper.
The first tree hit is nominative; brǣt hit has a reflexive accusative, and passive hit is nominative again.
Gestęnt remains singular in Old English; Cook identifies strong wind as second subject. English plural strike is idiomatic and does not alter the source.
Both feallan and hrēosan depend on onginnað.
Līegum follows Cook’s thunderbolt/levin gloss; it is not silently reduced to an ordinary indoor flame.
Three final subjects: high powers; this world’s wealth; earthly wonders.
Exact source geneahhe lacks the dictionary headword quantity mark; do not silently regularize.
